Training data-efficient image transformers & distillation through attention

kd>distilbert.lead: DistilBERT is the plainest application of Hinton's recipe to a pre-trained language model, with one change of timing that turned out to carry the result: the distillation happens during pre-training, not separately for each downstream task. The teacher's cost is paid once, by whoever publishes the model.

blocks.h: Why a masked LM distils well
blocks.b: Distillation's premise is that a teacher's softened output distribution carries the similarity structure the one-hot target throws away. For a masked language model that structure is unusually rich: the target at a masked position is a distribution over tens of thousands of word pieces, and the teacher's ranking of the alternatives is a statement about what the context admits. The hard label says the word was **bank**; the teacher says the slot also tolerated river, shore and vault, in that order, and rejected the rest. Training against the softened distribution therefore delivers many bits per example rather than one, which is why a student can reach a given quality in a fraction of the teacher's steps. The loss constrains outputs only, so the student is free to be a different shape.

blocks.h: What was halved and what was added
blocks.b: Sanh et al. halved the depth, six layers from twelve, kept the width and the tokeniser, and initialised the student by taking every other layer of the teacher — an initialisation that is only available because the width was left alone. Training used three losses: the usual masked-language objective, the distillation term against the teacher's softened distribution, and a cosine loss pulling the student's hidden states towards the teacher's. That third term is the one addition beyond the 2015 recipe, and it exists because output matching leaves the intermediate representation geometry entirely unconstrained, which wastes the fact that student and teacher share a layer layout. The next-sentence objective and the token-type embeddings were dropped. The result is around 40% smaller and roughly 60% faster at inference while retaining most of BERT's GLUE score.

blocks.h: What it settled and what it cost
blocks.b: Distilling once, before fine-tuning, made compression a publisher's step rather than a practitioner's, and a single small checkpoint served every downstream task. That is why the pattern stuck. Successors sharpened it: TinyBERT and MobileBERT showed that matching attention maps and hidden states layer by layer beats matching outputs, which is to say DistilBERT left capacity unclaimed by distilling mainly at the head. Two costs are structural. The student inherits the teacher's failure modes and its biases, and in this setup does not acquire capabilities the teacher lacks — though born-again and noisy-student results show a student can pass its teacher when the distillation signal is not the only one it trains on. And the economics shifted underneath it: once it became clear that a small model trained on far more tokens is strong on its own, distillation had to justify itself against simply training the small model properly.

refs.t: DistilBERT, a distilled version of BERT: smaller, faster, cheaper and lighter
Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network

lora>llama.lead: This arrow does not describe an influence on design. LoRA played no part in how LLaMA was trained, and Meta's paper does not depend on it. It is here because low-rank adaptation is the reason that releasing those weights had the consequences it did: it turned a checkpoint of seven to sixty-five billion parameters into something a single researcher with one GPU could actually change.

blocks.h: Freezing the base, learning a delta
blocks.b:
Hu et al. began from the observation that the update learned during fine-tuning has low intrinsic rank — the direction a task moves a pre-trained weight matrix is far simpler than the matrix itself. So freeze $W_0$ and learn $\Delta W = BA$ with $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$ and $r$ typically between 4 and 64:

$$h = W_0 x + BAx$$

The headline saving in trainable parameters understates the real one, which is optimiser state: Adam holds two moment estimates per trainable parameter, so freezing the base removes the dominant term in training memory along with the gradients and most of the cross-device traffic. And because $BA$ has the same shape as $W_0$, it can be folded into the weights after training, so inference costs nothing extra — the point on which LoRA beat inserted adapter layers, which add depth and latency.

Touvron et al.'s contribution was orthogonal: training only on publicly available corpora, and pushing small models far past the compute-optimal token count so that inference rather than training is the cheap part. Those two things met immediately. Within weeks of the February 2023 release, instruction tuning of the 7B and 13B models was being done with low-rank adapters on single consumer cards, and QLoRA — quantising the frozen base to four bits and training higher-precision adapters on top — brought fine-tuning of the largest model onto one 48GB GPU later that year. What LoRA supplied is the missing half of accessibility. Open weights that nobody outside a well-funded lab can afford to modify are a read-only artefact; open weights plus a method that fits on a gaming card are a platform.

blocks.h: What that made possible, and what it cost
blocks.b: The consequence was a derivative ecosystem rather than a model: instruction-tuned, domain-tuned and language-specific variants appearing faster than they could be catalogued, and a research literature that could finally run controlled experiments on a strong base model. Two costs came with it. Rank is a genuine limit — low-rank updates adapt style, format and instruction-following well, and are much weaker at installing substantial new factual knowledge, so the claim of parity with full fine-tuning holds on some benchmarks and not others. The second is sharper: safety alignment is itself a thin layer over a capable base, and cheap adaptation strips it as cheaply as it adds anything else. The property that democratised adaptation also made guardrail removal a weekend project, and no amount of care in the base model's training changes that arithmetic.

lora>ldm.lead: LoRA was written about GPT-3 and evaluated on language models; its arrival in image generation was a community port rather than a follow-up paper. The target was also narrower than the original method's. What gets wrapped in Stable Diffusion is chiefly the cross-attention projections inside the denoising U-Net — the small set of matrices where text meets pixels.

blocks.b: Rombach et al. condition generation by cross-attention inside the U-Net: the prompt is encoded once, and at several spatial resolutions the image features form queries while the text embedding forms keys and values, so $W_Q$ reads from the latent and $W_K, W_V$ read from the prompt. Almost everything about how a word maps onto appearance is carried by those projections. That localisation is what made low-rank adaptation such a good fit, and it is a property of the LDM architecture rather than of LoRA: the thing a user wants to change — what a particular style, subject or face looks like when named — lives in an identifiable subset of the weights instead of diffusely across the network. DreamBooth, by contrast, fine-tunes the whole U-Net and emits a multi-gigabyte checkpoint per concept.

blocks.h: What the port kept and changed
blocks.b: It kept $W_0 + BA$ unchanged, and kept the merge-at-inference property. What changed was which matrices get wrapped and the resulting scale: ranks of 4 to 32 over the attention projections produce files of a few megabytes rather than several gigabytes. That put LoRA between the two existing options — textual inversion, which learns only a new token embedding and is therefore bounded by what the frozen model can already draw, and full fine-tuning, which has the capacity but not the portability. The unplanned property was composition. Because an adapter is an additive delta, several can be summed with scalar weights at generation time, $W_0 + \sum_i \alpha_i B_i A_i$. This is not principled — the deltas were trained independently, they interfere, and concepts bleed into one another — but it works often enough to have become the normal way the model is used.

blocks.h: What it changed, and the bill
blocks.b: Distribution changed shape. A style or a subject became a shareable few-megabyte file rather than a model, repositories accumulated tens of thousands of them, and the base checkpoint turned into a substrate that other people build on. The technical costs are mild: unmerged adapters add inference overhead, stacked ones degrade unpredictably, and there is no way to tell in advance which pair will conflict. The social cost is not mild. The cheapest and most common use is imitating a named living artist, or a specific real person, from a few dozen images and an hour on a rented GPU. That is what moved the consent question away from the abstract composition of training corpora and onto a concrete file with a name attached. Neither source paper anticipated the use, and neither could have prevented it.
